Abstract: Sample efficiency is critical for online Reinforce-

While existing works investigate sample-efficient

tasks in another. Secondly, informative evaluation can also
be obtained from well-trained LLMs, such as GPT, LLaMA
and Gemini (Achiam et al., 2023; Dubey et al., 2024; Team
et al., 2024). For certain tasks, such models can provide
evaluation closely aligned with human preferences; see e.g.,
Ji et al. (2023); Lee et al. (2023). Lastly, there are scenarios where rule-based or heuristic reward functions—built
upon experts knowledge and accumulated experience—are
inexpensive to obtain and instructive in evaluating the LLM.
Taking summarization tasks as an example, expert summaries are available on datasets such as XSum (Narayan
et al., 2018) and TL-DR (V¨olske et al., 2017). Similarity
with those expert solutions can be measured through metrics
such as ROUGE (Lin, 2004) and BERTScore (Zhang et al.,
2019), and be employed for scoring the LLM generations.
Motivated by these considerations, this paper studies how
imperfect reward models can be used to learn a near-optimal
policy with fewer human annotations. We consider the case
where several source reward models are available, yet their
quality, i.e., the similarity to human rewards, is unknown a
priori. Our contributions are summarized as follows.
• In Sec. 3, we identify a distinctive property of RLHF arising from its KL regularization: for any prospective policy
candidates, its coverability for the optimal policy improves

Can RLHF be More Efficient with Imperfect Reward Models? A Policy Coverage Perspective
2. Preliminary
In this section, we review the mathematical formulation of
RLHF for LLMs and introduce our reward transfer setting.
2.1. Mathematical Formulation of RLHF
We adopt the contextual bandits framework (Lattimore &
Szepesv´ari, 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022), where we treat the
prompt space as the state space S and the response space as
the action space A. Without loss of generality, we assume
that both |S| and |A| are finite. We denote ρ ∈∆(S) as the
prompt distribution. An LLM can be modeled by a policy
π : S →∆(A), where, given a prompt s ∈S, the responses
are generated from the conditional distribution a ∼π(·|s).
Throughout this paper, we assume that all considered LLM
policy π have positive support over the entire state-action
space, that is, mins,a π(a|s) > 0. This is ensured in practice
by the softmax layer in LLM architectures.
Reward Model and Preference Model A reward model
is a function r : S × A →[0, R], where R is a constant
indicating the largest possible reward value. In the RLHF
setting, the reward r is unobservable and we can only access
its induced preference model, denoted by Pr. Pr(y|s, a, ea)
denotes the probability that a is preferable to ea given s (y =
1) or not (y = 0), by reward model r. Following previous
works, we consider the Bradley-Terry (BT) model (Bradley
& Terry, 1952): Pr(y = 1|s, a, ea) = σ(r(s, a) −r(s, a′)),
where σ(x) := 1/(1 + e−x) is the sigmoid function.
RLHF Learning Setting Given a reward model r, in the
context of RLHF for LLMs, the policy π is learned to
maximize the expected reward E[s∼ρ,a∼π(s), ea∼π(s)] [r(s, a) − r(s, ea)].

2.2. Reward Transfer in RLHF
We now describe the reward transfer setting. We consider
multiple source reward models {r1, r2, ..., rM} and the
ground-truth human reward r. The source reward models may
be misspecified, i.e., r_i is not exactly equal to r, but
have some unknown quality. We assume that for any s ∈ S
and a ∈ A, r_i(s, a) is known, but r is unknown. This is
a common scenario in practice, e.g., the LLM can be queried
for any r_i(s, a). The ground-truth human reward r is
unavailable, but can be inferred from the dataset. We denote
r as the true reward model that we aim to learn to maximize.

2.3. Policy Coverage and KL Regularization
We recall the policy coverage property induced by the KL
regularization in RLHF. In the standard RLHF framework,
the policy π is updated to maximize the expected KL regularized
RLHF objective:

π ∗ = argmax π E[s∼ρ,a∼π(s), ea∼π(s)] [r(s, a) − r(s, ea)] −
λ D_KL(π(s) || π_prev(s)),

where λ is the regularization coefficient, and π_prev is
the previous policy. This KL regularization enforces a form
of policy coverage, as it encourages the policy to explore
states where π_prev(s) is not too concentrated.

2.4. Self-Transfer Learning and Policy Selection
Motivated by the policy coverage property, we propose two
principles for transfer learning in RLHF: (1) selecting transfer
policy π_transfer with the highest policy value; (2) involving
the offline policy π_off computed with online collected data
as a candidate (self-transfer learning). 

The first principle leverages the fact that higher policy values correspond to better performance, and thus selecting the policy with the highest value reduces the regret. The second principle considers the offline policy computed with the data from the online learning process as a candidate, which we term as "self-transfer learning".

We then propose an algorithm named Transfer Policy Optimization (TPO) that implements these principles. At each step, TPO selects the transfer policy from a set of candidates based on their estimated policy values. In the early stages, when one of the source rewards is of high quality, TPO can significantly reduce the cumulative online regret. After a finite time, the self-transfer mechanism ensures that the regret grows at a rate of eO(√T), independent of the structural complexity measures.

2.5. Empirical Algorithm

Inspired by the principles, we propose an empirical algorithm named Transfer Policy Optimization (TPO) with an adaptive policy selection strategy. At each step, TPO selects the transfer policy from a set of candidates based on their estimated policy values. In the early stages, when one of the source rewards is of high quality, TPO can significantly reduce the cumulative online regret. After a finite time, the self-transfer mechanism ensures that the regret grows at a rate of eO(√T), independent of the structural complexity measures.

We further propose an adaptive policy selection strategy that picks the transfer policy with the highest estimated policy value. In the early stages, when one of the source rewards is of high quality, TPO can significantly reduce the cumulative online regret. After a finite time, the self-transfer mechanism ensures that the regret grows at a rate of eO(√T), independent of the structural complexity measures.

2.6. Computational Efficiency

We design an algorithm with improved computational efficiency, making it scalable to practical RLHF scenarios. In particular, we employ an Upper-Confidence Bound (UCB) subroutine to select the transfer policy with the highest win rate competing with the online learning policy. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated for fine-tuning T5 models on summarization tasks in Section 6.
